title: Enterprise SLO policy for top (protected) API routes: eligibility, targets, and exception handling
creator: Nikhil Sharma
description:
## Context
We need an explicit, auditable policy for which Hosted API routes qualify as “protected” (enterprise-priority capacity protection) and what SLO behavior we commit to during fleet/regional pressure.

This ticket defines:
1) Protected route eligibility criteria and initial route list
2) Tier semantics + measurable SLO targets (availability + latency signals)
3) Error budget + alerting alignment with SRE
4) Exception / contractual commitment process (temporary burst, permanent overrides, customer-specific caveats)

Motivation:
- 2025-11-03 Sev1 (fleetwide latency cascade from a single hot route) showed we cannot rely on “best effort fairness” across shared GPU pools.
- Enterprise teams are asking for predictable behavior and clear 429 semantics under overload.

## Definitions
**Protected route**: a route group that receives (a) reserved admission budget under pressure, (b) priority routing, and (c) explicit SLO dashboards/alerts for the enterprise tier.

**Tier classes (Hosted API):**
- Enterprise: SLA-backed customers (contract includes availability + support response, plus explicit overload behavior)
- Standard: paid self-serve (best-effort under pressure)
- Free/Trial: best-effort + earlier throttling

**What protection is (and is not):**
- Is: predictable throttling/shedding order; enterprise preserved longer; clear 429 reason codes; faster detection + mitigation.
- Is not: unlimited capacity; a guarantee that enterprise never sees 429s during extreme load; a pricing/billing change.

## Eligibility criteria (route qualifies for “protected”)
A route is eligible if it meets ALL:
1) Material enterprise usage (>= 3 enterprise tenants OR >= 20% of enterprise token volume in a region)
2) Has historically contributed to fleet pressure (tail latency amplification, queue depth spikes, or error burst correlation)
3) Has a stable contractable interface (clients can implement retry/backoff; semantics won’t churn weekly)
4) Can be measured in a low-cardinality way (route group attribution supported; no per-customer metric explosion)

A route is NOT eligible (for now) if:
- It’s experimental/preview and not part of enterprise SLA
- It has highly variable runtime characteristics with no agreed measurement envelope
- Protecting it would require per-tenant hard reservations in the runtime scheduler (out of scope for this initiative)

## Initial protected route list (MVP)
Route groups (logical grouping may include aliases/versioned endpoints):
1) **Chat / text generation**
   - /v1/chat/completions
   - /v1/completions (legacy, if mapped to same backend)
2) **Embeddings**
   - /v1/embeddings
3) **Rerank**
   - /v1/rerank

Notes:
- If /v1/responses is enabled for a subset of tenants, it should be treated as “Chat” for protection only when it becomes GA for enterprise.
- Fine-tuning and file endpoints are explicitly excluded from protected scope.

## SLO targets (enterprise tier only, protected routes)
We are defining SLOs that (a) map to how the platform fails under overload, and (b) are measurable/alertable.

### Availability SLO
**Target**: 99.9% successful requests per route group, per region, rolling 28 days.
- Success includes: 2xx + streamed completions that terminate normally.
- Excludes: customer-caused auth failures (401/403), invalid requests (400), and customer-side cancellations.
- Includes as errors: 5xx and “unexpected” 429s (see 429 policy below).

### Latency SLO (operational, used for paging + internal review)
We will track and alert on latency separately from the public “availability” SLO.
**Enterprise latency objective (per route group, per region):**
- Chat: p95 TTFT and p99 end-to-end latency dashboards, with burn alerts keyed off regression vs baseline.
- Embeddings/Rerank: p95/p99 end-to-end latency.

Rationale:
- The absolute ms target depends on model + prompt/output sizes and is hard to contract generically. We will operationalize with baselines per model family and enforce that overload protection prevents tail-latency blowups.

### Overload behavior objective
During regional/fleet pressure, we expect:
- Best-effort tiers shed earlier (predictable 429s) to preserve enterprise budgets.
- Enterprise tiers may see 429 only when enterprise budgets are exhausted or when safety limits prevent queue death spirals.

## 429 semantics policy (enterprise vs best-effort)
We will standardize 429 reasons in gateway responses and document retry/backoff.

**Enterprise 429s:**
- Allowed reasons:
  - quota_exceeded (contracted quota)
  - burst_limit_exceeded (configured burst)
  - over_capacity (only when enterprise admission budget is exhausted OR safety backpressure triggers)
- Requirement: responses must include reason + recommended retry headers.

**Best-effort 429s:**
- Expected under pressure (over_capacity) and must be earlier/more predictable than 5xx/latency collapse.

**Policy for counting 429s in availability SLO:**
- For enterprise protected routes:
  - quota_exceeded and burst_limit_exceeded do NOT count against Redwood availability SLO (they are customer-config / contractual caps).
  - over_capacity DOES count against availability SLO and should page when sustained (this indicates we failed to protect enterprise traffic sufficiently).

## Error budget + alerting alignment
- SRE will own SLO dashboards and burn alerts per protected route group and region.
- Paging policy:
  - Page on enterprise over_capacity 429s sustained above threshold OR enterprise 5xx burst OR severe latency burn.
  - Do NOT page on best-effort shedding alone (informational annotation only).

## Exception handling / contractual commitments
We need a consistent, auditable exception process for enterprise accounts.

### Types of exceptions
1) **Temporary burst increase** (time-bound)
   - Use case: launch week, migration, backfill.
   - Default duration: 7–30 days with explicit expiry.
2) **Permanent burst / quota override**
   - Use case: contract addendum, dedicated capacity mapping, special integration.
3) **Route protection expansion**
   - Use case: enterprise wants a non-MVP endpoint protected.
   - Requires eligibility review + SRE sign-off.

### Required inputs for any exception
- Customer + account ID(s)
- Route group(s)
- Region(s)
- Requested burst/quota numbers
- Expected workload shape (RPS, token rates, prompt lengths, concurrency)
- Justification and expiry (if temporary)
- Risk assessment: impact to other enterprise tenants and fleet

### Approval + ownership
- Temporary burst: Solutions Engineering + SRE on-call delegate + Product (Hosted API) approval
- Permanent override: Product + Exec sponsor (Platform or Reliability) approval
- Any exception that materially changes protection budgets: requires SRE sign-off (to avoid silent SLO erosion)

### Customer communication requirements
- We must describe the change as “capacity protection / predictable overload behavior” (avoid overpromising “guaranteed priority” unless contract language explicitly says so).
- Provide documented retry guidance and reason codes.

## Deliverables
- Route group list and eligibility criteria documented in Confluence (linked in ticket)
- SLO policy: what counts in/out, and 429 counting rules
- Exception workflow: who approves what + where it is tracked (Linear + Support macros)
- Sign-offs captured in comments

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Protected route list defined (MVP) with clear eligibility criteria
- [x] Enterprise SLO policy written (availability + 429 counting rules) and reviewed by SRE
- [x] Exception handling process defined, including approvals and expiry for temporary burst overrides
- [x] Alignment with customer messaging ticket (FAQ) and Support playbook work
comments: 2025-11-21 (Nikhil Sharma): Drafted initial eligibility criteria + proposed MVP route list (chat/embeddings/rerank). Added explicit non-eligibility conditions to avoid “protect everything” drift.

2025-11-25 (Sean Gallagher): SRE request: availability SLO must explicitly define how 429s are treated. Specifically, enterprise ‘over_capacity’ should count against SLO; quota/burst should not. Also please avoid hardcoding latency ms targets in policy—use baselines + burn alerts.

2025-11-26 (Rafael Mendes): +1 on separating contractual SLO (availability) from operational latency objectives. We can page on latency burn without putting absolute ms numbers into the contract language.

2025-12-02 (Dev Patel): Support needs a crisp exception workflow: when a customer complains about 429s, we need to know whether it’s quota/burst vs overload. Please ensure we have reason codes and a rule for escalation (e.g., enterprise over_capacity sustained > X mins).

2025-12-04 (Nikhil Sharma): Updated policy to add exception types (temporary burst, permanent override, protection expansion) and an approval matrix. Added comms guidance (“capacity protection” framing).
2025-12-06 (Neha Kapoor): Approved direction. Please ensure any permanent changes that increase enterprise budgets require explicit SRE sign-off to prevent silent error budget erosion across regions.

2026-01-10 (Chris Osei): Marking as Done after Confluence SLO policy page was published and referenced by PM-883/Support docs. Remaining work is execution (ENG + Support), tracked in dependent tickets.
